items.claim: A server returning 200 for an arbitrary Host header is not by itself a vulnerability; the finding survives only when the unrecognised host changes the response content, produces a redirect, an absolute URL to an attacker domain, or a password-reset link built from the host.
items.disproof: It IS exploitable when the response body, Location header, or any absolute link differs between a legitimate host and an attacker-controlled host; it is a non-finding when every host value yields byte-identical status, headers and body, because a 200 on an unknown vhost is normal virtual-host routing behaviour.

sources.quote: Since the host and port information acts as an application-level routing mechanism, it is a frequent target for malware seeking to poison a shared cache or redirect a request to an unintended server.
By default, the server will respond to requests for any hostname, including requests addressed to unexpected or unconfigured hostnames.

items.body: Mechanism: A server returning 200 for an arbitrary Host header is not by itself a vulnerability; the finding survives only when the unrecognised host changes the response content, produces a redirect, an absolute URL to an attacker domain, or a password-reset link built from the host. How to apply it in the field: treat this as the fp_rule it is — a hunter must be able to state the concrete observation that demonstrates it, with a request and response in hand, before the finding is reportable. Boundary of the rule: It IS exploitable when the response body, Location header, or any absolute link differs between a legitimate host and an attacker-controlled host; it is a non-finding when every host value yields byte-identical status, headers and body, because a 200 on an unknown vhost is normal virtual-host routing behaviour.

items.claim: The convincing host-header validation is a request/response pair where a reset or confirmation email is requested while sending a foreign Host, and the response body contains an absolute link or token-bearing URL pointing at the attacker's domain rather than the legitimate one.
items.disproof: If the emitted URL always uses a server-side configured canonical domain regardless of the Host sent, the pair fails and the injection does not exist; if the endpoint is unauthenticated but the URL is still server-derived, this is not host-header injection at all.

sources.quote: The "Host" header field in a request provides the host and port information from the target URI, enabling the origin server to distinguish among resources while servicing requests for multiple host names.
Controls whether the server requires the requested hostname be listed enumerated in the virtual host handling the request

items.claim: Calling a reflected host value 'web cache poisoning' overstates it unless a caching layer actually keys on that host value, so the report must show a cache in front or a backend that caches by the supplied host before the class can be claimed.
items.disproof: It IS cache poisoning when a shared cache keys responses on the attacker-supplied host or absolute URL and later serves that poisoned entry to other visitors; it is NOT when the response carries no-store or private cache directives, or when the application is fronted only by a per-user browser cache the attacker cannot write to.

sources.quote: An interception proxy is particularly vulnerable if it relies on the host and port information for redirecting requests to internal servers, or for use as a cache key in a shared cache, without first verifying that the intercepted connection is targeting a valid IP address for that host.
The ngx_http_proxy_module module allows passing requests to another server.

items.body: Mechanism: Calling a reflected host value 'web cache poisoning' overstates it unless a caching layer actually keys on that host value, so the report must show a cache in front or a backend that caches by the supplied host before the class can be claimed. items.claim: When an application trusts X-Forwarded-Host or equivalent proxy headers to build absolute URLs, the control that must exist is a list of hops whose forwarding headers are honoured, and the bypass is sending that header directly from outside that list and getting it reflected.
items.disproof: It is not a bypass when the edge proxy strips or overwrites client-supplied X-Forwarded-Host before it reaches the application, or when the application only reads the proxy header from a connection whose peer address is inside the trusted hop list; if the header is unconditionally trusted from any source, the allowlist control is absent entirely.

sources.quote: The ngx_http_realip_module module is used to change the client address and optional port to those sent in the specified header field.
While this is convenient, it is sometimes desirable to limit what hostnames a backend application handles since it will often generate self-referential responses.

items.body: Mechanism: When an application trusts X-Forwarded-Host or equivalent proxy headers to build absolute URLs, the control that must exist is a list of hops whose forwarding headers are honoured, and the bypass is sending that header directly from outside that list and getting it reflected. items.claim: An attacker-controlled hostname appearing inside an absolute URL in a response body is not an open redirect, because the user must still act on a link whose destination is chosen by the application; the class is open redirect only when the server itself issues a 3xx whose Location the attacker controls.
items.disproof: It IS an open redirect when a request parameter or header is reflected into the Location header of a 302 or 301 and the browser follows it off-site; it is not when the host appears only in body content the client renders as text, in which case the correct finding is host-header injection or content injection rather than redirection.
